title: Contains Duplicate III
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every nearby pair versus a sliding window combined with value bucketing.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums and two integers indexDiff and valueDiff, return true if there exist two DIFFERENT indices i and j such that abs(i - j) <= indexDiff and abs(nums[i] - nums[j]) <= valueDiff.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Nearby index\" plus \"nearby value\" simultaneously","A sliding window (for the index constraint) combined with value-bucketing (for the value constraint)"],["\"Within valueDiff\" check","Bucketing values into buckets of size (valueDiff+1) makes same-bucket membership an automatic match, and only adjacent buckets need a direct check"]]}

blocks.text: The indexDiff constraint means only a SLIDING WINDOW of the most recent indexDiff elements ever needs to be considered. Within this window, the valueDiff constraint can be checked efficiently by bucketing values into fixed-size buckets: two values in the SAME bucket are automatically within valueDiff of each other, and only the immediately adjacent buckets need an explicit check.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking for Nearby Similar-Priced Items Within a Recent Time Window
blocks.text: Picture checking whether any two items sold within a recent time window (indexDiff) also have similar prices (valueDiff). Grouping prices into fixed price BRACKETS makes it instant to know if two items in the same bracket are close enough, and only bordering brackets need a quick direct comparison.

blocks.caption: Bucketing values into fixed-size ranges makes same-bucket membership an automatic match

blocks.text: Result: true. Indices 0 and 3 (both value 1) satisfy |0-3|<=3 and |1-1|<=0.

Before checking every pair within indexDiff directly, notice that maintaining a sliding window of size indexDiff, and bucketing the values within it, lets each new element be checked against the window in O(1) using bucket lookups instead of O(indexDiff) comparisons.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Only pairs with abs(i-j) <= indexDiff matter, so maintaining a sliding window of the last indexDiff elements (plus the current one) is sufficient.

Observation 2: Bucketing values into buckets of size (valueDiff+1) means any two values in the SAME bucket automatically satisfy abs(value difference) <= valueDiff.

Observation 3: Two values in ADJACENT buckets might also satisfy the value constraint, so those need an explicit check, but no other buckets could possibly qualify.

Observation 4: As the window slides, remove the bucket entry for the element leaving the window, keeping the bucket map always representing exactly the current window's contents.

This leads to maintaining a sliding window (of size indexDiff) via a bucket map: for each new element, check its own bucket and the two adjacent buckets for a valid match, then insert it and remove the expiring element's bucket entry.
Check every pair of indices within indexDiff of each other directly for the value constraint.
Why the code is written this way

items: Checking only nearby indices already respects the indexDiff constraint directly.
This still costs O(n times indexDiff), which can degrade to O(n squared) when indexDiff is large.

blocks.text: Limitation: bucketing values within a sliding window achieves O(n) instead of O(n times indexDiff).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Maintain a hash map from bucket id to the value stored there, representing the current sliding window of size indexDiff. For each new element, compute its bucket id; if that bucket is occupied, an automatic match is found; otherwise, check the adjacent buckets (id-1 and id+1) directly, since those are the only OTHER buckets that could contain a valid match. Insert the new element's bucket entry, and remove the entry for the element now leaving the window (indexDiff positions back).

Maintain a bucket map representing the current window. For each element, check its own bucket (automatic match) and adjacent buckets (explicit check); insert its bucket, remove the expiring element's bucket.
Dry run for nums = [1, 2, 3, 1], indexDiff=3, valueDiff=0 (bucket width 1)

Bucketing values into ranges of size (valueDiff+1) guarantees that any two values landing in the SAME bucket automatically satisfy the value constraint, and any valid match with a DIFFERENT bucket can only come from an immediately adjacent bucket (since buckets further away are guaranteed to differ by more than valueDiff). Maintaining this bucket map as a sliding window of size indexDiff (removing the expiring element's bucket entry) ensures only valid index-nearby elements are ever considered.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(min(n, indexDiff)) for the bucket map.

blocks.text: Contains Duplicate III is a strong example of combining a sliding window (for the index constraint) with value bucketing (for the value constraint) to achieve O(n) for a problem with two simultaneous proximity conditions.

items: Using a bucket width of valueDiff instead of valueDiff+1, causing off-by-one errors in matching.
Forgetting to handle negative values correctly in the bucket id computation.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "nearby index AND nearby value simultaneously", think: sliding window for the index constraint, bucketing for the value constraint.

items: How would you solve this using a balanced BST (ordered set) instead of bucketing?
Any "two simultaneous proximity constraints" problem, solvable via sliding window plus bucketing.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Checking every nearby pair costs O(n times indexDiff) time; the sliding window plus bucketing approach costs O(n) time and O(min(n,indexDiff)) space.

items: Pattern: sliding window (index constraint) combined with value bucketing (value constraint).
Core Idea: bucket values into ranges of size valueDiff+1; same bucket is an automatic match, adjacent buckets need a direct check; slide the window by removing expiring bucket entries.
Time: O(n times indexDiff) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: bucketing turns a value-proximity check into an O(1) lookup instead of a linear scan.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, non-obvious combination of two techniques.
One line memory trick: bucket by value (width valueDiff+1), slide window by indexDiff, check same/adjacent buckets.
